g_time_confound.explanation: Our nets run in numpy (nn/numpy_net.py: 3x3 convs as tensordot -> OpenBLAS). The arena uses 14 spawned workers; each imports arena.tournament, which imports numpy at module load, before _init() sets OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 (setdefault, and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS is never set). OpenBLAS therefore starts its default pool (16 threads) in every worker -> up to 14 x 16 BLAS threads on 16 cores. A 6x64 forward pass (tensordot over 64 channels) is large enough for OpenBLAS to multithread, so it suffers; the 2x32 distills' matrices are small enough to stay single-threaded (2.0 ms in the arena = 2 ms measured alone). Torch bots (bruneton_az) call torch.set_num_threads(1) in _init and are unaffected. This is an inference from the code plus the timings above; it was not re-run with BLAS pinned to 1 thread inside the arena.
g_time_confound.affects_strength: No, as far as the code shows: our MCTS bots use a fixed 200 simulations and play deterministically (no time control; no move hit the 300 s timeout; 0 forfeits), so the same moves would have been played at ~0.3-1 s/move. The confound matters only for any 'equal wall-clock' claim: none can be made from this run.
g_time_confound.equal_budget: Nominally equal search budget between our MCTS nets and bruneton_az: 200 PUCT simulations each, fresh tree every move, exact terminal values in both. Differences: c_puct 1.5 (ours) vs 1 (bruneton), centre-first vs random tie-break, and bruneton's net is 2.6x larger (1.20 M vs 0.458 M params), so its per-simulation compute is higher, not lower. plkmo_az used 777 reads and alfo_mcts 3000 random-roll-out iterations: not equal budgets. Policy-only nets use no search.

supported: Among the 19 non-solver bots of part3, nn_sup_6x64_mcts200 has the highest point-estimate Elo (1761, CI 1718-1814). Its lead is significant over every neural net except our own az_6x64 (see suggestive). Against the open-source AlphaZero net bruneton_az the gap is +180 Elo (bootstrap CI +143 to +217, P>0 = 1.000) and head-to-head 27-5-7 (score 0.756, CI 0.637-0.868).
Better than our PPO/DQN/distilled nets: sup - ppo_from_sup = +170 Elo (CI +134 to +207).

Its policy head alone is the most accurate move predictor we have: optimal 0.907 vs 0.727 (az), 0.786 (ppo_from_sup), 0.838 (dqn) on the same 1000 solver positions; with MCTS200 0.940 vs 0.834 (az). (Note dqn: high 'optimal' but low arena Elo - per-position accuracy alone does not rank bots.)
suggestive: sup vs az (our self-play net): +43 Elo, bootstrap CI +6 to +82, P(sup>az) = 0.988; head-to-head 23-2-15, score 0.600 (CI 0.487-0.725), sign test p = 0.256. Top-15 pool: +33 (CI -9 to +72). Without the two near-trivial openings: +55 (CI +13 to +98). Not robust: the interval includes 0 in at least one analysis and/or the direct match is not significant, so 'better than our AlphaZero net' is NOT established; the full-pool gap comes partly from results against weaker bots.

Elo cannot separate sup from perfect play (sup - pons = -28, CI -63 to +8), but sup is not perfect: against pons (40 games, expected score 0.5 from the opening values) it scored 0.412 (13-7-20), i.e. it gave away 3.5 of 20 available points; az_6x64 gave away 5.5 and bruneton_az 11.5. The Elo tie only means the 20-opening pool cannot tell them apart (pons' Elo is capped by its lost openings).

Solver blunder rates (fraction of own moves that change the game-theoretic result): sup 0.0203, az 0.0282, bruneton 0.0584, ppo_from_sup 0.0562. These are over different positions (each bot reaches its own), so they are descriptive, not a controlled comparison.

Why (hypothesis): supervised training on perfect solver labels gives a better prior and value than 12.3 h of self-play at this size, and MCTS200 adds most where the prior is good (ladder +653 for sup vs +97 for az). Confounds: sup and az differ in data, training length, and the sup net was selected on bench_optimal (best.npz); one run each, no seeds.
needed_experiments: Re-run the top neural bots with BLAS pinned to 1 thread (OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 before numpy import) and add an equal wall-clock condition (e.g. 1 s/move for every MCTS bot, bruneton_az included), plus bruneton_az at 800+ sims; this settles whether the ranking is about the net or the budget.
More openings (e.g. 100-200 instead of 20) for the sup vs az vs bruneton vs pons sub-pool: the CI on sup - az is driven by 20 opening clusters per pairing.
Size/signal ablation: train az and sup at identical size, steps and seeds (>=3 seeds each), and put sup/az policy-only and az+MCTS100 (the distillation teacher) into the arena.

regressions.x: log10 arena ms/move (confounded by BLAS oversubscription)

distill_vs_teacher.missing: part3 has neither az_6x64 policy-only nor az_6x64 + MCTS100 (the actual teacher), and no 6x64 vs 2x32 pair trained the same way. So the student-vs-teacher gap and the pure size effect cannot be read from the arena; the methods table (ladder Elo, 100 games each) has az policy-only 1547 vs student 1579 and optimal 0.727 vs 0.724.

findings.title: Elo reproduced
findings.claim: Re-implemented Bradley-Terry + cluster bootstrap reproduces the stored part3 Elo of all 20 bots to within 0.05 points (CI bounds within 0.0).
findings.caveat: CI bounds depend on the resampling order; reps = 500, seed 0.

findings.title: Our supervised net beats the open-source AlphaZero net
findings.claim: nn_sup_6x64_mcts200 is +180 Elo above bruneton_az (CI +143 to +217); head-to-head score 0.756.
findings.caveat: Same nominal budget (200 sims) but different code (c_puct, tie-break); bruneton's 'best' weights as shipped; one weight file only.

findings.title: Supervised vs self-play net
findings.claim: sup vs az (our self-play net): +43 Elo, bootstrap CI +6 to +82, P(sup>az) = 0.988; head-to-head 23-2-15, score 0.600 (CI 0.487-0.725), sign test p = 0.256. Top-15 pool: +33 (CI -9 to +72). Without the two near-trivial openings: +55 (CI +13 to +98).
findings.caveat: One training run each; differ in data, size of training and checkpoint selection.

findings.title: Not distinguishable from the solver by Elo
findings.claim: sup - pons_perfect = -28 Elo (CI -63 to +8); vs pons directly sup scored 0.412 in 40 games.
findings.caveat: Elo of a perfect player is capped by lost openings; see openings table.

findings.title: Search helps most for the best prior
findings.claim: MCTS200 adds +653 to sup_6x64, +97 to az_6x64, +107 to ppo_6x64, +330 to ppo_from_sup, +521 to pilot_cpu_sup, +466 to pilot_cpu_az ladder Elo (methods table); in the arena ppo_6x64 gains +172 (CI +138 to +208).
findings.caveat: Ladder Elo extrapolates from near-100 %% scores vs minimax d1-d8 (100 games): 2180 for sup+MCTS is far outside the ladder (max d8 = 1500) and not comparable to arena Elo.

findings.title: Time per move is a hardware artefact
findings.claim: Our MCTS200 nets averaged 67 s/move in part3 vs 0.29 s in the methods table (~232x); policy-only 6x64 nets ~0.49 s vs 2.9 ms; bruneton_az 0.78 s.
findings.caveat: Explained from code (BLAS thread oversubscription), not re-measured inside the arena; fixed-sim search means strength is unaffected, but no equal-time claim can be made.

findings.title: Who throws away won positions
findings.claim: Share of own moves that change the solver result: sup 2.03 %, az 2.81 %, bruneton 5.84 %, pons 0 %. Share of moves in won positions that give the win away: sup 1.99 %, az 2.28 %, bruneton 6.64 %.
findings.evidence: best_nn.decomposition.f_blunders (every move of every game solved, weak mode)
findings.caveat: Each bot faces different positions; rates are descriptive.

findings.title: Best single predictor of arena Elo
findings.claim: Of the non-Elo measurements, elo_vs_keeps_nl predicts arena Elo best (all series, R^2 = 0.59, n = 12); 'optimal' is weaker (R^2 = 0.32). The other strength measure, methods-table ladder Elo, has R^2 = 0.89 (Spearman 0.97) but compresses at the top (slope 0.65).
findings.caveat: n = 8-20 points, one run per method; bootstrap slope CIs are wide and R^2 differences between predictors are not significant.

findings.title: Tournament health
findings.claim: 7599 of 7600 games played (1 missing: bruneton_az vs nn_sup_6x64_mcts200 opening 0), 0 forfeits; our three MCTS200 nets used 95 % of all thinking time.
findings.caveat: Think time is reconstructed from per-game averages.

findings.title: Opening set: values and two near-trivial openings
findings.claim: Solver values of the 20 openings for the first player: 9 win, 3 draw, 8 loss. 2 openings (3344, 4626) end in <= 9 plies in 78 %/78 % of games: the side to move has an immediate, unstoppable threat, so ~10 % of all games carry almost no information about skill (sup lost 31 of its 96 losses there).
findings.caveat: Openings are random 2-4 ply sequences (seed 4150) filtered only for mirror duplicates; a new opening set should exclude positions with a forced win in <= 3 moves.
